https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.text: The Hungarian parliament building on the banks of the Danube is not being lit as normal at night owing to energy-saving measures being imposed during drought conditions View image in fullscreen The Hungarian parliament building on the banks of the Danube is not being lit as normal at night owing to energy-saving measures being imposed during drought conditions The Sunday read Climate crisis Destroyed crops, riverbed cyclists and a ‘Rock of Starvation’: how drought has devastated the Danube The Guardian travelled 100 miles along the EU’s longest river, where some residents are struggling to secure drinking water Lorenzo Tondo in Hungary. Photographs by David Levene Sun 16 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 00.01 EDT Share For centuries, the rock was seen as a warning. When it began to emerge from the Danube, beneath Gellért Hill in Budapest, it meant the river had fallen so low that floating mills could no longer operate, crops were probably failing, and hunger would almost certainly follow. That is why, in the Hungarian capital, where over time the boulder became little more than a legend, it was named Ínség-szikla – the Rock of Starvation. Today, amid record-low water levels on the Danube, the rock has not only emerged from the water, but surfaced almost in its entirety, along with the sandy riverbed on which it rests, astonishing geologists and government scientists sent to examine it. And, much as the rock was said to warn, Hungary is now facing an unprecedented energy crisis that has forced the country to shut down all but one of its Danube-cooled nuclear reactors for the first time in 44 years. The Guardian travelled for more than 100 miles (160km) along the banks of the Danube, the EU’s longest river, which sustains the 10 countries it crosses, visiting villages and towns where residents are struggling to secure drinking water and farmers are fighting to keep their crops alive. Map of Danube River Pócsmegyer Last week, the Hungarian prime minister, Péter Magyar, warned that the economic damage caused by this year’s drought was expected to surpass that of the historic dry spell that devastated Hungary’s farmland in 2022. View image in fullscreen István Somogyi has lost nearly 50% of his harvest this year While the full extent of the losses is still difficult to assess, István Somogyi, a 56-year-old farmer from Pócsmegyer, a village on the Danube, in Pest County, has already done his calculations. View image in fullscreen “I’ve lost nearly 50% of my harvest this year and it could go up to 70%,” he said. “It’s gone. Everything has dried up. Since I started farming this land after the end of communist rule, I’ve never seen a catastrophe like this.” Somogyi said the unprecedented crisis did not come out of nowhere, and that the heatwaves and droughts of previous years had already offered a warning. Scientists say that human-caused climate breakdown is making every heatwave in the world more intense and more likely to happen. “You could see this coming,” he said. “The harvest was already poor last year. But we were lucky because the Danube stayed high. Despite the intense heat, there was still enough water in the soil. This time, there is no hope of saving our crops.” On the near-deserted roads running alongside the river, families with children sought relief in the Danube’s shallow waters, while, not far away, military water tankers were siphoning water from rural wells, hauling vital supplies to the storage pools that feed the local grid. Szentendre View image in fullscreen Low water levels in the Danube at Szentendre Across the river from Pócsmegyer, on the opposite bank of the Danube, lies Szentendre, a town known for its community of artists. During the most intense days of the heatwave, some evening performances have been held by candlelight in an effort to reduce electricity consumption. View image in fullscreen Aerial view of a long boat filled with people in shallow water Here, in recent weeks, vast, desert-like islands have emerged. The exposed riverbed is cracked like a mosaic of hard, dry clay, baked by suffocating heat that has pushed temperatures in Budapest close to 42C , with overnight temperatures hitting a high of 28C. Europe is warming faster than any other continent, with intense summer heat and prolonged drought being amplified by the deepening human-caused climate crisis. Extreme conditions continue to fuel wildfires and strain water supplies. View image in fullscreen József Gulyás stands in front of stocks of bottled water being kept at the town hall in case of supply shortages In some stretches of the Danube near Szentendre, it is now possible to walk through it with the water barely reaching above your ankles. “Swimming and navigation are banned here,” said László Balázs, 44, head of the local river rescue service. “But people escaping the heat still enter the water, unaware it can suddenly drop into deep pools where they risk drowning.” At the end of June, Budapest police (BRFK) said three people had gone missing in the Danube over a single weekend. Water police later recovered one body near Iváncsa, while searches continued downstream for the other two missing swimmers. The drought and resulting disruption to energy supplies have also left some Hungarian towns struggling with shortages of drinking water. In a room inside Szentendre’s tourist information office, thousands of bottles of water are stored ready to be distributed, particularly to elderly and vulnerable residents. “About 4,000 to 5,000 households were left without water,” said József Gulyás, 62, Szentendre’s deputy mayor. “We distributed 25 tonnes of water and received about 100 emergency calls a day. We had never experienced anything so serious. Elderly women would hug the officers delivering water and burst into tears.” Budapest View image in fullscreen A geologist takes advantage of the low water levels view the ‘Rock of Starvation’ Driving from north to south, towards the Hungarian capital, Budapest, where the level of the Danube under normal conditions reaches an average height of 2 to 3 metres, and can rise as high as 8 metres, intense summer heat and continuing drought conditions caused the river to fall to a record low of just 14-19 cm on 4 August. Nazi shipwrecks emerge from the depths as Europe’s Danube dries up Read more Average daily water level, cm The water levels have fallen so dramatically that, as the Danube has retreated, it has revealed a succession of relics long hidden beneath its waters, including the remains of a woolly mammoth , a bridge destroyed after the second world war in Budapest, a Nazi warship and an unexploded British bomb . View image in fullscreen Tourists and passersby look down over the side of the Liberty bridge in Budapest. The remains of an older bridge can be seen the shallow waters below. The water is so low in the capital that on 28 July, at about 4.30pm, Gábor Kürti, president of the Magyar Kerékpárosklub (Hungarian cyclists’ club) and owner of a cargo bike company, left his office in central Budapest, jumped on his bicycle and, in an unprecedented feat, rode for 30km along the exposed bed of the Danube, with his journey quickly going viral on social media . View image in fullscreen Kürti rode for 30km along newly-exposed beds of the Danube “I wanted to show that if you can cycle along the bed of the Danube for 30km, it means that, because of this climate emergency, we have literally hit rock bottom,” he told the Guardian. Riding his KTM X-Strada 20 gravel bike, Kürti set off from the mouth of the Szilas stream (Szilas-patak) and made his way across fine gravel, large pebbles, hard-packed sand and mud, eventually reaching the ferry terminal at Vác about three hours later. “For many people it was an extraordinary adventure. For me, it was heartbreaking,” he said. “Cycling through parts of the river where, as a child, I used to swim or go kayaking, and which I could now cross on a bicycle, filled me with an indescribable sadness. It was like looking at the scene of a terrible accident. Throughout that journey, the scale of the catastrophe was unfolding before my eyes.” Nagytétény View image in fullscreen The Kis-Háros-sziget island nature reserve is usually only accessible by boat but is now reachable by foot, as low water levels in the Danube have exposed the river bed connecting the island to the mainland Kürti took the Guardian into what, until only a few months ago, was the striking floodplain forest in Nagytétény named Kis-Háros-sziget, a protected area home to climbing plants, wild vines and several families of European beavers. The river is reached by walking across ground that would normally lie several metres beneath the water. Here, one branch of the Danube has receded so dramatically that it came to an abrupt halt, blocked by an exposed riverbed left behind by the drought. Its dry, clay-like surface looks like an image from a future shaped by the escalating human-caused climate crisis. Yet this is happening now. Passersby walk across what was once the river, their feet sinking into patches of mud. Kayakers struggle to make their way through the remaining shallow channels; many eventually give up, lift their kayaks on to their shoulders and walk home. Hungarian authorities have been pumping water into large areas of the country’s nature reserves such as the one in Nagytétény, to keep marshlands from drying out as the drought intensifies. Paks View image in fullscreen Hungary’s only nuclear power station, in Paks near to the banks of the river Danube Continuing south, the road finally reaches Paks, home to Hungary’s nuclear power plant, its towers rising above the horizon. Here, municipal workers have been working weekends to keep more than 700 threatened trees alive and water the town’s flowerbeds. View image in fullscreen Szilvia Farkas: ‘I have never seen so much vegetation dry out in all my years doing this job.’ “I’ve been doing this job for 18 years,” said Szilvia Farkas, 39, who is employed by Dunakom Zrt in Paks, owned entirely by the municipality, to plant and water trees and plants. “I have never seen so much vegetation dry out in all my years doing this job, and I have never worked as hard as I have this year to try to keep it alive.” Dunakom Zrt uses its own drilled well for water extraction. In addition, the company is able to extract water from a decantation basin. The public is not permitted to use tap water for irrigation at the moment; instead, residents collect greywater and use it to water their gardens. In the country’s more marginalised and deprived areas, the water crisis has compounded longstanding problems for thousands of people who were already living in difficult conditions before the drought, struggling with inadequate access to running water and sewage systems. Géza Orsós Renáta, 43, who lives with her four children in a small farmhouse on the outskirts of Paks, has never had access to running water. Orsós, who also works for Dunakom Zrt, helping to water public green spaces drying out in the heat, has long relied on water from a neighbour. View image in fullscreen Géza Orsós Renáta is helping to water public green spaces drying out in the heat “Even in winter, we have to pump water and heat it in large bowls so we can wash,” she said. “Now a friend brings us water once a week. But it is becoming unbearable.” Driving back from Paks, tall, swollen clouds occasionally gather on the horizon in the clear skies above Budapest, appearing to promise the return of rain, only to fade by evening, dashing the hopes of an entire country. For now, people can do little but cling to the hope that the Rock of Starvation will disappear once more beneath the currents of the Danube, returning to the depths of the river and becoming little more than a legend again. But Somogyi, who grew up hearing the story of the boulder passed down through generations, and who is now witnessing the consequences of the warning it was said to foretell, knows it will not. “The drought will return next year,” he said. “That is the trend. And there isn’t much that we can do.” Explore more on these topics Climate crisis The Sunday read Drought Rivers Hungary Europe Water Share Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

In a statement issued late on Tuesday, the BFU said the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner started its takeoff at Munich Airport at 1:57 pm (1157 GMT) on Saturday and was late getting into the air. It said the tail touched the ground just before lift-off and that tire marks had been found at the end of the runway that were probably from the aircraft. The plane eventually turned around, landing back at Munich Airport at 3:58 p.m. The agency said its experts were currently analyzing the plane's flight recorders and that authorities in Vietnam and the US were also participating in the investigation. "The investigation does not serve to establish blame, liability or claims," the authority said, but rather was intended to help prevent any such accidents and incidents in future. Experts have said that the 270 passengers and crew on board the plane narrowly escaped disaster. The aircraft had great difficulty taking off despite the pilot's efforts to pull the nose up. Passengers and crew were uninjured. https://p.dw.com/p/5J4ov Skip next section Tenants should be able to install heat protection more easily — justice minister 08/19/2026 August 19, 2026 Tenants should be able to install heat protection more easily — justice minister Laws on rented accommodation could potentially be changed to allow tenants more freedom in adapting their apartments to cope with heat ways, Federal Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig has said. "Conventional legal policy can also make a contribution to heat protection," she told the daily Rheinische Post in an interview published on Wednesday morning. "I am thinking about tenancy laws in particular," she said. "I can imagine, for example, that we make it easier for tenants to equip their apartments with air conditioning or sun shades." At present, tenants have no legal right to install built-in air conditioning devices or external shades but need permission from their rental owner. Hubig also spoke out in favor of the proposal made by her Social Democratic Party to enshrine climate protection in the German constitution, or Basic Law , as a joint obligation of both the federal government and state administrations. Currently, the primary responsibility for heat protections lies with the states and municipalities. "This would make it easier for the government to give states and municipalities sustained support in heat-protection measures," she said. Germany, like much of ‌Europe, has experienced ⁠successive ⁠heat waves this summer with temperatures repeatedly approaching 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit). Donaustahl CEO Stefan Thumann told private broadcaster RTL and magazine Stern in a joint interview that he had received warnings from German officials in late 2025 that Russian intelligence was plotting against his life. "I'm fighting a duel with the Russian military intelligence service for my life," he said. "Constantly changing locations, 24-hour personal security, my private life has ceased to exist," he added. Thumann said he now slept next to his computer and started working as soon as he woke up to distract himself from his personal situation. In March, prosecutors said they had arrested two so-called disposable agents who were alleged to have spied on Thumann to prepare an assassination attempt. Disposable agents is the name given to people with little training who are hired by military intelligence services for small pay to carry out missions. But RTL cited a German lawmaker who said there were still plans targeting him that were well advanced and involved using a nerve agent. The group discussed Ukraine’s air defence needs and a winter support package. Photograph: Francisco Seco/AP View image in fullscreen US envoys (from left) Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv. The group discussed Ukraine’s air defence needs and a winter support package. Photograph: Francisco Seco/AP Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: US envoys leave Kyiv without breakthrough on ending war Zelenskyy says after talks with Witkoff and Kushner that Kyiv seeking ‘serious volumes’ of US support for winter defences. What we know on day 1,657 Guardian staff and agencies Sun 6 Sep 2026 21.33 EDT Last modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 21.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have held “encouraging” talks with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv in their first official visit to Ukraine but made no breakthrough towards ending the war with Russia. The envoys’ trip followed talks with Russia’s Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday which a Kremlin aide said were “highly useful” while also giving no indication of a breakthrough. Zelenskyy said at a news conference that his talks with the envoys on Sunday covered air defence needs – including Patriot systems – and a “winter package” of support covering both air defence and energy infrastructure before the colder months. He said Kyiv was seeking “serious volumes” of American support on that front, with backing from European partners as well. It appeared the war would continue into winter, he also said. Zelenskyy said Russia had intensified strikes on Ukrainian cities before Russia’s State Duma election later this month, calling the attacks deliberate “terror” against civilians. Ukraine was working with 67 domestic companies developing systems to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered drones at scale. He said the sides agreed to hold a follow-up meeting involving Ukraine, the US and Europe, with a location still to be set. The US envoys brought new and “more effective” proposals to Ukraine on ending the war with Russia , according to one senior Ukrainian presidential official. “It’s not the same as it was before. This one now is more effective,” the unnamed offical told Agence France-Presse after the talks with Zelenskyy. “They’re still talking. This is actually the most important part. There are three of them now.” Ukraine’s rail operator announced the envoys’ departure from Kyiv early on Monday. Witkoff said earlier that both sides would need to compromise , adding: “We think we have the ingredients to get to that place … and we look forward to continuing this as long as it takes.” Kushner said: “Hopefully this trip has come out with some new ways to advance forward. I think we’ve learned a lot from the trip.” In Moscow the US envoys had “ discussed substantive plans which will be announced in the coming weeks” , a White House official said. The Kremlin said the Americans had “put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement”, without elaborating. Witkoff said he was hopeful a new round of US-mediated Ukraine-Russia talks would be announced “in short order”. Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine while Zelenskyy insists Russia should not be rewarded for its aggression. A girl ⁠was killed and three ⁠other people ⁠were wounded ​in a Ukraine ⁠drone attack on the Russia-held Black ⁠Sea port ​city ‌of Sevastopol ‌late on ‌Sunday, the city’s Moscow-appointed governor, Mikhail Razvozhayev, said on Telegram. Russian forces ⁠struck ​a ‌Ukrainian ‌cargo vessel in ‌the Black Sea which was carrying ​military equipment supplied to ⁠the Ukrainian ​army by ​western ​countries, Russian ​news ‌agencies ​reported the defence ministry as saying on ​Sunday. Kyiv’s forces struck the Ryazan oil refinery – about 480km (300 miles) inside Russia – causing a fire, Ukraine said on Sunday. Russia’s foreign minister said Germany’s accusation that Moscow was involved in a ⁠drone incident near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport were, “by and large, the ⁠start of a real war”, state news ​agency Tass ‌reported. “He is, in effect, declaring war on us,” Sergei Lavrov said of the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz. Berlin has ordered a series of measures in ​response to the attack attempt. Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP View image in fullscreen Rescue workers put out a fire at a residential building destroyed by a Russian missile strike on Kyiv, Ukraine, on Wednesday. Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP European Union EU leaders to press Burnham to pay more towards Ukraine’s defence Officials will call on UK to ‘step up’ financial support at Brussels summit – with post-Brexit issues also on agenda Jennifer Rankin in Brussels Fri 23 Oct 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 02.37 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google EU leaders will press Andy Burnham at a summit in Brussels to contribute more to Ukraine’s defence effort in 2027. EU officials argue that the UK, Canada and Japan should do more to support Ukraine , but entreaties to these G7 countries for extra financial aid at recent international meetings have not been answered, Brussels says. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen , will call on the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, to contribute to Ukraine’s looming financial shortfall at an EU-Canada summit in Montreal next week. A similar request to the British prime minister will be made when he meets von der Leyen and the European Council president, António Costa, for a long-awaited EU-UK summit on 20 November in Brussels. It comes as the UK chancellor, John Healey, prepares for his first budget next week, weighing numerous calls for more spending against the rising cost of government borrowing and a darkening economic outlook. Healey said earlier this month he was “working on different ways we can step up support for Ukraine – military, diplomatic and economic”. View image in fullscreen Firefighters tackle a fire in a residential building after a Russian drone strike on Kramatorsk on Thursday. Photograph: Diego Herrera Carcedo/Anadolu/Getty Images Ukraine says it faces a €70bn (£58bn) funding shortfall in 2027 to pay for its defence and civilian needs. The EU and its member states are paying for 80% of Ukraine’s financial needs, according to the commission, which considers a “fair” EU share to be two-thirds, with the remaining third covered by other allies. “We will continue to lead, but we urgently need other partners to step up,” von der Leyen told reporters last week, without naming countries. The EU last year agreed a €90bn loan for Ukraine, intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv’s funding in 2026 and 2027. But as Russia escalates its attacks, dragging the war into its fifth winter, Ukraine’s costs continue to spiral. EU officials have prioritised non-EU G7 countries, above all the UK, Canada and Japan. But they are now casting the net wider and may look to Switzerland, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand to promise additional aid to Ukraine. The British government says it has committed £25bn to Ukraine, including £16bn in military aid. The UK is Ukraine’s fourth largest donor, behind the US, Germany and France, according to the Kiel Institute’s Ukraine Support Tracker . But the picture changes when the UK’s share is weighted to GDP. The UK was assessed by the Kiel researchers as spending 0.86% of national income to support Ukraine, compared with 1.1% from France and 1.5% from Germany. These three large European economies spent significantly less than the Nordics and Baltics, such as Denmark (4.2%) and Estonia (3.8%). The UK is more in line with France and Germany when their contribution to EU programmes is stripped out. The UK government has been contacted for comment. The European Commission declined to comment on specific countries, but referred to a recent statement: “We always said that we cannot walk this alone … therefore our partners in general must step up.” View image in fullscreen A Kyiv shopping mall damaged by a Russian missile strike on Thursday. Photograph: Sofiia Lavska/Apostrophe/Global Images Ukraine/Getty Images Ukraine will be one of several issues on the agenda at the EU-UK summit, where leaders are expected to conclude three agreements: a food and animal health (SPS) deal to reduce Brexit paperwork; the linkage of the EU and UK emissions trading schemes (ETS) to protect British industry from European carbon taxes; and a youth mobility scheme to enable 18- to 30-year-olds to live, work, travel and study across both sides of the Channel. In a positive sign for British negotiators, the European Commission proposed deferring the question of university tuition fees, one of the last big sticking points. The UK would like to charge EU students at British universities the international rate, about four times higher than the domestic fee. The EU, where many officials are alumni of British universities, wants to return to the pre-Brexit status quo, when EU students paid home rates. Commission officials have proposed resolving this thorny question in technical talks within six months of the 20 November summit, rather than risk derailing the high-profile leaders’ meeting. But senior EU sources are confident they still have leverage on the issue, as the SPS and ETS deals will not come into force until there is a youth mobility agreement acceptable to the European side, including on tuition fees. “The three elements are a sort of gift to the UK, but not a massive gift,” an EU diplomat said, adding that the EU would still have clout in the negotiations over the fees. “The leverage is that the UK needs this [the other agreements].” UK hopes to strike economic security agreements with the EU , to avoid British industry becoming collateral damage of Europe’s defensive measures against China, are seen as another source of leverage. But a second diplomat said there was no consensus among the EU’s 27 member states on postponing the tuition fees question until after the summit: “There is no clear majority saying ‘let’s drop it now for six months’,” they said.
